A girl sits on a high cliff,
her eyes wander over the wide, murky sea;
tear after tear falls on her withered face:
and there she weeps day after day;
there the sun greets her when it rises;
there it bids her farewell when it sets behind the mountains.

White vapors creep over the water,
like the billowing sails of a ship:
they confuse the maiden with deceptive images.
He does not go; alas, your beloved does not go:
is he a prisoner among the Muslims,
or has he already given his soul for the holy faith? —

The king announced the cross and the trumpets sounded,
the victorious youth were called to war,
across the wide sea, to the Holy Land:
and the hero did not know how to resist,
lest he go there to fight the holy battle,
where the cross was thrown into the dust by the Muslims.

“Farewell, girl, gray dove!
But therefore do not cloud your eyes:
I already have a cross and a sword, faith calls to battle:
when that meadow turns green again,
I will return to you again, beloved soul:
and then forever, forever you will be mine.”

And the meadow turned green again;
but in vain the girl wound
her wreath into the wedding wreath:
even the beauty of the meadows fell crookedly with a scythe,
only the desolate autumn bloomed in the meadow:
and she still has no lover and no lover. —

And she sits on a high cliff,
her eyes wander over the wide, murky sea;
tear after tear falls on her withered face.
The sun has already set; the evening breathes frost,
and the sea beneath her sways freely;
the moon looks into the sea, young.

And what is that floating across those murky waters?
Is the swan still breeding on the sea,
and with her mother her dear family? —
No; the swan does not breed on the sea:
it is time for that, since she has nestled herself in the thick reeds at the foot of the mountain.

The hero is pale there, floating on the water,
the sign of the cross is red on his cloak;
a bullet in his chest, a broken sword in his fist:
and when the maiden caught sight of the hero,
she fell soullessly from the high cliff:
oh, it was him, her beloved.

Thousand years ago from the second layer of times
You already stood, castle, on the heights,
Under Slavomir already the victors of the kingdom
They were quite famous in Orava,
In your crown of copper cups
They were toasting here in honor of the Templars.


Where is Donča's wild hand hidden,
That he disfigured his own wife?
Where lies the hard heart of Hippolytus,
That he killed his little daughter?
Where are the Hussites' echoes of the psalms,
Where are their trumpets — who will tell us?


As a bee has one small leaf,
When there is a storm, it will be useful,
So here too have Polish nobles often found shelter
On the roads.
You fed strangers, you took them under your roof,
For your own good you fell into ridicule.


Where is that little soul, who with the beauty of an angel
Overcame the monastery walls,
With a pure heart she knew how to win,
Where the piety of the spirit could not.
Thurza, Barbara are covered by the grave rocks,
Sparks from their deeds only where they remained here.


Castle, you are the image of a true Slovak —
Your gates are distorted!
You listened to the Czech, the Hungarian, the Pole,
You bred the Silesian with the Italians.
While you were in glory, they slapped you,
Now, impoverished, everyone has abandoned you.


You are a shabby leopard, but you are not an orphan,
The rock still stands firm —
In your hill a star twinkles,
That will calm your heart.
Let you be half dead — when it shines on you,
Your ravaged spirit will fly to heaven.

What have you done to Athens, Socrates,

That the people carry your golden statue,

Having first poisoned you...

What have you done to Italy, Alighiera,

That the insincere people will build two tombs for you,

Having first banished you...

What have you done to Europe, Columbus,

That he digs three tombs in three places,

Having first chained you...

What have you done to your own, Camoens,

That the grave digger shakes your grave for the second time,

Having first starved you...

What have you, Kościuszko, done to the world,

That two boulders crush you on either side,

Without a place first...

What have you done to the world, Napoleon,

That you were locked in two tombs after your death,

Having locked you in two tombs First...

What have you done to people, Mickiewicz?...

So it doesn't matter in what urn you will rest,

Where? When? In what sense and form?

For they will open your grave again,

They will proclaim your merits differently,

And they will be ashamed of the tears you shed today,

And they will shed tears of a second power for you,

Those who could not see you as a human being...

The world cannot

Accept everyone like you at once to a peaceful bed,

And it never accepted, like age upon age,

For clay melts into clay without ceasing,

When contradictory bodies are nailed together,

Later... or first…

A certain rabbi in the Talmud, bathing up to his ears,

Suffering from a flea biting him; he finally becomes indignant:

He continues to lie in wait, caught. He sits pressed,

He spins, stretching his head and knives:

"Forgive me, Rabbi, it is not fitting for a wise man to be angry:

Can blood be shed on a descendant of Levites?"

"Blood for blood!" the Rabbi shouted, "Belijala is giving birth!

Philistine, fattened at the expense of others!

Ants build granaries; industrious swarms

They bring honey and wax, and poisonous drinks:

You alone among men bustle with liquor,

You drunkard, all the more harmful because you drink what is foreign."

He finished, and as he mercilessly choked the prisoner,

The dying Flea squealed: "And what does the Rabbi live on?"

You, impious Death, have violated my eyes,

That I saw my dear child dying!

I saw her once shaking a ripe fruit,

And the hearts of her unfortunate parents were broken.

She would never have been without great sorrow,

My own death could never have been without heaviness,

And heartfelt pain, in any summer,

She would have departed from me sadly in this world;

But I have never mourned her death,

Never been sadder or more melancholic.

And she, if God had willed, could have increased her age

The power of consolations before my eyes with a longer age.

And at least in the meantime I could have passed

My own age and presented myself to Persephone last,

Without feeling so great a sorrow in my heart,

Which I do not see in this mortality.

I don't blame Niobe for turning to stone when she looked at the dead bodies of her beloved children.

"So, love, love, love knows no season, but don't lose your mind like the wise Solomon, Samson was left without eyes, a man will resemble a beast because of the love drive. Happy is he who does not love. Orpheus, who enchanted the beasts, threw away his flute with a wonderful tone and for the sake of spirit, imagine, decided to go down to Pluto. And Narcissus, in the forest shelter, took a peek into the water and fell there without a cry, without a groan. Happy is he who does not love. David, the wisest among kings, forgot God's law and got tangled in a woman's fleece; he left his war horse and took a sable, and Sardanapalus wrapped himself in a soft tunic... No, there is no reason in love. Happy is he who does not love. The lustful Amnon surpassed all in sins, Tamar, his sister, preferred as a depraved pharaoh; for a lustful dance before his throne, King Herod, the scourge of Zion, cut off the head of John. Happy is he who does not love. For whose sake, guess, did he change my whole style and sweep the floor with me?… For Catherine Vossel, excuse me! I hope that that farfaron — Noel — will catch a glimpse of him under the whip or even on some branch. Happy is he who does not love. Message What should this impudent vagabond do today, you say? No, no, put him on the stake, but he will love Villon again! He will be a windbreaker again and will run after petticoats again, Cupid is not joking… Happy is he who does not love."

"My soul felt that I would lose her forever… And the escape began! My wonderful escape from Italy! In a crowd of kilometers… On the landscapes, torn muscles in the dark! The threat that I would lose my Italy grew constantly in the brutal — and so helpless — flight through cities… We lost! We lost Venice forever! (And in our photos tomorrow it will mercilessly prove its absence to us). How the oranges shone coldly on their black branches… How the radiant names of cities and rivers flew into the sky… Castles! (Highway-Cathedral.) The nights in hotels — and the pain in my eyes…
When she bowed before my eyes with the operatic grace of a statue. Ah, that so distant... stuffed Italy... Give me back Italy! Give me back Italy! The beautiful and youthfully sunny Italy! Which I saw most unexpectedly on the most childish of my childhood mornings... She sang - so whole - and danced, and how her Roman ankles and steps shone on the orange peels in the basin of the Burgas harbor... But I grieve for Venice... Let's run away! I can't live without Italy!"

Callisthenes, a youth in Athens,
once came from a swarming night
with a withered wreath of ivy around his wild hair
in the morning twilight to his home,
certainly paler than the pale twilight of the morning.

When now his servant to his bedroom
lights him through the high colonnade,
with a full and strong torchlight
there appears the marble statue of Bacchus,
a glorious work, created by the hand of a master.
In the fullness of youth the god rises
with the rich, long-rolling splendor of locks
and the lushly swelling wreath of grape vines.

The pale apprentice stands in awe,
with his eye blinded by the god's brilliance,
it seems to him that the high son of Zeus
touches his forehead with his thyrsus staff
and speaks to him these angry words:
"Why do you stagger here, deprived of strength and sanity,
a shadow from dark Erebus!
You have desecrated my ivy wreath
and foolishly call yourself my priest.
Depart from me, I do not know you!
I am the fullness of creative nature,
which in its divine power
reveals itself most richly in the blood of the noble grape.
If your desolate life needs a God,
then do not seek him where in the glare of the sun
the full vines cover the mountain slope,
no, seek him deep in the dark night of Hades!"

And the god is silent, the torch goes out.
Callisthenes goes to his bed in shame,
he lays aside the withered ivy wreath,
and quietly, deep in his heart
he incants a sacred word of promise.
